chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Abu Yusuf Ya'qub ibn Abdillah, from the descendants of Abu Fatimah, from Isma'il ibn Zayd, the freedman of Abdillah ibn Yahya al-Kahili, from Abdillah ibn Yahya al-Kahili, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

A man came to the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) while he was in the Mosque of Kufa, and said: 'Peace be upon you, O Commander of the Faithful, and the mercy and blessings of God.' He replied, and the man said: 'May I be your ransom, I intended to go to Al-Masjid Al-Aqsa, so I wanted to greet you and bid you farewell.' He (AS) asked him: 'What did you intend by that?'

He said: 'The reward (fadl), may I be your ransom.' He (AS) said: 'Then sell your mount, eat your provisions, and pray in this mosque, for the obligatory prayer in it is an accepted Hajj, and the voluntary prayer in it is an accepted Umrah.'

And the blessing from it extends for twelve miles: its right side is good fortune, and its left side is cunning. In its center is a spring of oil, a spring of milk, a spring of drinking water for the believers, and a spring of pure water for the believers. From it sailed the ship of Noah (peace be upon him), and it contained Nasr, Yaghuth, and Ya'qoq. Seventy prophets and seventy successors prayed in it, and I am one of them.

And he (AS) placed his hand on his chest and said: 'No distressed person who supplicates in it with a request for any of the needs will be left unanswered by God, nor will He fail to relieve his distress.'

key_terms.الْمَسْجَدَ الْأَقْصَى: Al-Masjid Al-Aqsa (The Farthest Mosque, often referring to Jerusalem or used comparatively for high virtue)
key_terms.حَجَّةٌ مَبْرُورَةٌ: An accepted Hajj (one whose sins are forgiven)

ai.seo_question: What are the virtues and rewards of praying in the Mosque of Kufa according to Imam Ali (AS)?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam Ali (peace be upon him) responds to a traveler’s inquiry about the virtues of the Mosque of Kufa, establishing a profound theological equivalence between local devotion and the major pilgrimage rites. The Imam highlights the unique metaphysical attributes of the site—such as the springs of oil, milk, and water—and emphasizes its role as a sanctuary where the supplications of the distressed are swiftly answered, reflecting the Shia emphasis on the intercessory and spiritual potency of the Imams' resting places.
